I have resolved the issue where email messages crashed on non-ASCII domain names when the email encoding was non-unicode.

### Cause of the Issue
When constructing the `Message-ID` header, [`EmailMessage.message()`](file:///testbed/django/core/mail/message.py#L240-L265) uses `make_msgid(domain=DNS_NAME)`. If the computer's hostname or the domain contains non-ASCII characters (e.g., unicode characters), [`socket.getfqdn()`](file:///testbed/django/core/mail/utils.py#L14-L17) returns a non-ASCII hostname string. In non-unicode encodings like `iso-8859-1`, [`forbid_multi_line_headers`](file:///testbed/django/core/mail/message.py#L55-L71) attempts to encode the `Message-ID` header using the email's encoding, raising a `UnicodeEncodeError`.

### Solution
1. In [`CachedDnsName.get_fqdn`](file:///testbed/django/core/mail/utils.py#L14-L18), encode the hostname returned by `socket.getfqdn()` using IDNA (`.encode('idna').decode('ascii')`) to convert internationalized domain names (IDNs) to ASCII-compatible encoding (ACE/punycode).
2. In [`EmailMessage.message`](file:///testbed/django/core/mail/message.py#L258-L270), convert the domain name to IDNA/ASCII before passing it to `make_msgid()`, ensuring that non-ASCII domain names (even if patched or overridden directly) are IDNA-encoded and valid in ASCII for the `Message-ID` header.
